problem: VLM-based navigation systems either query the VLM continuously (high latency and memory cost) or rely on end-to-end RL or dense semantic mapping (poor sim-to-real transfer, heavy compute). VLMs also lack the geometric precision needed for collision-free continuous control.
motivation: Indoor robots need both semantic understanding (e.g., find the doorway out of the room) and precise geometric control on edge hardware. The paper separates slow, sparse semantic reasoning from fast deterministic control so the VLM is only used at key decision points.
key_idea: A five-state finite-state-machine Chain-of-Thought (Search, Find, Scan, Navigate, Recover) queries a small VLM only at decision points, uses Grounded-SAM plus camera projection geometry for target and obstacle localization, and uses proportional visual servoing over 3D waypoints, with no dense mapping.
insight: Successful episodes need only 1-3 VLM calls, and the more difficult scenarios need more calls plus recoveries and collisions, which suggests the FSM keeps the VLM off the continuous control path. There is no ablation or baseline comparison, so the claims about efficiency and the benefit of the design are supported only by these per-scenario statistics.
method: FSM-CoT: five states (Search, Find, Scan, Navigate, Recover), each with its own prompt template, so the FSM holds the context and no long dialogue history is needed; the VLM is called only in Search and Recover.
Search: the VLM checks the RGB frame for the target (e.g., a doorway); if it is not visible, the agent scans with nine 10° rotations at 0.3 s intervals.
Find: Grounded-SAM segments the open-vocabulary target with up to 3 refinement passes, and the image coordinates are projected into the 3D camera frame.
Scan: the camera tilts down 40°, Grounded-SAM segments obstacles, and they are projected into 3D; if an obstacle lies within a 0.50 m margin, a bypass trajectory is planned, otherwise a direct one.

Navigate: proportional visual servoing follows 3D waypoints, with steering scaled by projected waypoint size; a waypoint counts as reached within 0.30 m, and every 15 steps the FSM returns to Scan to replan.
Recover: when the target is lost or the path is invalid, the VLM is re-queried to re-establish the objective.

Dual-isolated architecture: Habitat-Sim plus the geometric pipeline run in one environment and the VLM plus Grounded-SAM in another, connected by an asynchronous socket interface; the system fits in an 8 GB VRAM budget.

numbers_note: No standard benchmark is used, and no baselines are compared. Results are per-scenario means on 24 custom Habitat scenarios (no aggregate SR/SPL). Scenario-level mission success is 8/12 (Qwen3.5-2B) and 7/12 (Moondream2-2B). Scenarios 1-12 and 13-24 are different scenario sets, so the two VLMs are not compared on the same scenarios.
results: OptiSight completes 8/12 scenarios with Qwen3.5-2B and 7/12 with Moondream2-2B (a scenario counts as successful if at least half of its 10 runs succeed), using typically 1-4 VLM calls per episode. Several scenarios reach 100% success (Exp 03, 07, 09, 19, 20, 23, 24). No baseline is compared.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation on a single hard-coded instruction ('Get out of the room') in 24 custom scenarios, with no standard benchmark, baselines or ablations; no real-robot validation.

Many scenarios fail (0% success in several), especially with collisions, reflective surfaces, extreme viewpoints or ambiguity, and the 2B VLMs are weak; the evaluation also mixes different scenario sets for the two VLMs.
The efficiency claims (latency, 8 GB VRAM) are not quantified against continuous-query baselines.
